newsitem.title: USA: CME feeder cattle settle firmer on corn price drop.
newsitem.headline: CME feeder cattle settle firmer on corn price drop.

text.p: A late break in corn futures provided fresh support in the CME feeder cattle pit and futures again ran up for closing gains, traders said.
The late gains in feeders came after profit taking set prices back from futures early set new contract highs.
Live cattle futures closed firmer, buoyed by strength in cash beef prices, traders said.

Feeder cattle closed 0.400 cent per lb higher to 0.050 lower with August up 0.175 at 76.650 cents after setting a new high early of 76.800. May through November all set contract highs early. Live cattle ended 0.250 to 0.125 per lb higher with June up most at 65.475 cents. October posted a new high of 69.100 cents in late trade.

Selling during the day developed in live cattle after feeders jumped early to new highs. Some traders expressed concern the market may be overbought since the sharp price runup following storms and floods that caused heavy calf death losses in the northern Plains. Corn futures were also holding stronger than expected and sparked profit taking in cattle, traders said.
But futures held technical support and turned back up with a break in corn futures bolstering the late advance.
Traders expect strong demand for replacement feeders to continue following active fed cattle movement this week.
"They are moving cattle out and they want to refill the feedlot," said Dale Benson, vice president and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.
The latest CME feeder cattle index was up $0.17 at $72.32 per cwt.
Lind-Waldock bought August early while late demand was mixed, pit sources said.

The continued stronger-than-expected tone to boxed beef prices and active packer demand for fed cattle this week offset profit taking and continued scale-up commercial hedging interest to push live cattle higher late, traders said.
"Beef markets remain firm on better than expected movement today as retailers continue to book (boxed beef) for featuring into mid May and late May, which would include Memorial Day," Benson said.

Early resistance came on commercial hedging reflecting projected increased fed cattle supplies after record first quarter cattle placements. Some traders also said packers may pull from May contracted cattle to keep from having to pay higher prices again next week.
However, others noted there are not enough May contracted cattle to significantly weigh on prices.

Benson noted that the percentage of reported contract cattle to total fed cattle numbers was running below normal. Contracted cattle will not be plentiful enough to influence trade until June, he added.

Refco bought June and August while R.J. O'Brien sold. Cargill Investor Services bought June early and then traded on both sides of the market. Lind-Waldock spread long June/short August much of the day, pit sources said.
In live cattle options, volatility in June was down with commission houses selling 63 puts and 66 calls, pit sources added.
